newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Queen's man in Australia refuses death law delay.
newsitem.headline: Queen's man in Australia refuses death law delay.

text.p: Australian Governor-General Sir William Deane on Wednesday rejected pleas from two terminally ill people to delay signing an anti-euthanasia bill into law so they could legally kill themselves.
But the doctor who has already helped four terminally ill people take their lives said he would tell the other two how to do it without official help.
"I'll be certainly providing advice about that," Dr Philip Nitschke told reporters.
The federal bill, passed by parliament amid heated debate early on Tuesday, will strike down the world-first euthanasia law that the Northern Territory enacted in July.
"We weren't asking a great deal from the governor-general," said Nitschke.

"Really what they were saying was that a delay of a few days, at least a delay over Easter, would have given them a chance to work some of this out, to think through some of these very important decisions, and if they had wanted to, to go ahead and use the act over Easter."

But Deane, who represents Britain's Queen Elizabeth as head of state, felt a delay would be unjustified, although he had received letters and telephone calls urging one, his office said in a statement.
"...He considers that he would not be justified in departing from ordinary procedure in order to delay the commencement of the proposed law," said the statement from Government House.
Before the Senate passed the bill, pro-euthanasia senators tried to insert an exception to let two terminally people who had completed legal formalities kill themselves.
The bid failed, however, and the bill passed unamended to strike down the Northern Territory law as soon as Deane goes through the formality of giving it "the Royal Assent".
Nitschke said on Tuesday that the two dying people would write to Deane, asking for a delay of one or two weeks. One of them is a 56-year-old nurse suffering from cancer.
But governors-general, as unelected officials, very rarely depart from formal procedure. Most, including Deane, are former High Court judges.
Government House said the bill would normally be signed a day after all the paperwork was in, and the last of that arrived on Wednesday afternoon.

The four people who have legally killed themselves since the law came into effect in July used a computer-controlled machine that injected a lethal drug. The first was 66-year-old cancer sufferer Bob Dent, who died in September to avoid what he called "a roller-coaster of pain."
Euthanasia has remained illegal in the rest of Australia but supporters and opponents agree that it is widely practised.
The vote to strike down the territory law ignored the 75 percent majority of Australians who back euthanasia.
Prime Minister John Howard was one of the members of parliament who voted for the backbencher's bill in a conscience vote.
